glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: As the plagues strike Egypt’s livestock, bodies, and fields, the LORD declares that He has raised up Pharaoh to show His power and make His name known in all the earth, warns Egypt in mercy, and exposes Pharaoh’s confession as words without the fear of God.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Exodus 9 brings the fifth, sixth, and seventh plagues. The LORD continues to set Israel apart, as He began to do with the swarms of flies (8:22–23).

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Exodus 9:1–7 — The LORD Strikes Egypt’s Livestock and Spares Israel’s

  • Exodus 9:8–12 — Boils Break Out on Man and Beast

  • Exodus 9:13–21 — The LORD Declares His Purpose and Warns of Hail

  • Exodus 9:22–26 — Hail and Fire Fall on Egypt but Not on Goshen

  • Exodus 9:27–35 — Pharaoh Confesses Sin and Hardens His Heart Again

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “But indeed for this purpose I have raised you up, that I may show My power in you, and that My name may be declared in all the earth.” (Exodus 9:16)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The judgments grow heavier. A pestilence strikes Egypt’s livestock in the field while not one of Israel’s animals dies, and Pharaoh sends to confirm it and still refuses. Boils break out on people and animals, and the magicians who once copied Moses cannot even stand before him. Then, for the first time, the narrator says, “the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh” (9:12), as God had announced.

Before the hail, God explains His purpose: “for this purpose I have raised you up, that I may show My power in you, and that My name may be declared in all the earth” (9:16). Yet even this judgment comes with mercy. God warns Egypt to bring people and animals inside, and Pharaoh’s own household divides. Those who “feared the word of the LORD” make their servants and livestock flee into the houses, and those who ignore it leave theirs in the field. The storm strikes all Egypt, but not Goshen.

Pharaoh finally says the right words: “I have sinned this time. The LORD is righteous” (9:27). Moses is not deceived: “I know that you will not yet fear the LORD God” (9:30). When the storm stops, Pharaoh sins yet more and hardens his heart. Admitting guilt is not the same as yielding to God.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Exodus 9:1–7 — The LORD Strikes Egypt’s Livestock and Spares Israel’s

The LORD sends a severe pestilence on Egypt’s livestock in the field at a set time, but not one of Israel’s animals dies. Pharaoh confirms the difference, yet his heart becomes hard.

Exodus 9:8–12 — Boils Break Out on Man and Beast

Moses scatters furnace ashes toward heaven, and boils break out on people and animals throughout Egypt. The magicians cannot stand before Moses, and the LORD hardens Pharaoh’s heart as He had said.

Exodus 9:13–21 — The LORD Declares His Purpose and Warns of Hail

The LORD tells Pharaoh that He has raised him up to show His power and make His name known in all the earth, and He warns of hail unlike any Egypt has seen. Pharaoh’s servants who fear the LORD’s word make their servants and livestock flee into the houses, while others leave theirs in the field.

Exodus 9:22–26 — Hail and Fire Fall on Egypt but Not on Goshen

Moses stretches out his rod, and the LORD sends thunder, hail, and fire that strike people, animals, plants, and trees throughout Egypt. Only in Goshen, where Israel lives, is there no hail.

Exodus 9:27–35 — Pharaoh Confesses Sin and Hardens His Heart Again

Pharaoh confesses that he has sinned and that the LORD is righteous, and Moses prays so that Pharaoh will know the earth belongs to the LORD. Moses knows Pharaoh still does not fear God, and when the storm stops, Pharaoh and his servants harden their hearts again.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Exodus 9 holds together two truths that people often pull apart. The LORD hardens Pharaoh and declares a purpose for doing so, and Pharaoh hardens himself and remains responsible. Paul quotes 9:16 to show God’s freedom in judgment (Romans 9:17). The same sun that softens wax hardens clay, and the same pressure that should have humbled Pharaoh only set him harder against God.

The chapter also shows how people treat God’s word. In the same household, some feared His warning and brought their servants and livestock inside, and others ignored it and lost what they had in the field. Pharaoh’s confession is a sober lesson too: it is possible to say “I have sinned” under pressure without ever bowing to God.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
God’s name in all the earth. The LORD acts so that His power is seen and His name is declared everywhere (9:14, 16, 29).

Divine hardening and human responsibility. The LORD hardens Pharaoh, and Pharaoh hardens his own heart (9:12, 34–35).

Mercy within judgment. God warns Egypt so that people and animals can take shelter (9:19–21).

God distinguishes His people. Israel’s livestock and Goshen are spared (9:4, 6, 26).

Confession without repentance. Pharaoh admits sin but does not fear the LORD (9:27–30, 34).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
All the livestock (9:6). “All” here most likely means all within the scope announced, the livestock “in the field” (9:3). Egyptians still had animals to shelter from the hail (9:19–21).

The LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh (9:12). The first time the narrator says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh, fulfilling His word in 4:21. It stands beside Pharaoh’s own hardening (9:34).

Raised you up (9:16). God kept Pharaoh standing and in power so that His power and name would be displayed through the confrontation.

Feared the word of the LORD (9:20). Taking God’s warning seriously enough to act on it. Some of Pharaoh’s own servants did.

focus: Exodus 9 brings three more plagues on Egypt: a pestilence on the livestock, boils on man and beast, and the heaviest hail Egypt had ever seen. As the judgments intensify, the LORD declares His purpose that His name be proclaimed in all the earth, warns Egypt in time to take shelter, and exposes Pharaoh’s confession as words without fear of the LORD.

sections.title: The LORD Strikes Egypt’s Livestock and Spares Israel’s
sections.summary: The LORD announces a severe pestilence on Egypt’s livestock “in the field” (Exodus 9:3) and sends it at the set time, so that “all the livestock of Egypt died” (Exodus 9:6) but not one of Israel’s animals dies. Pharaoh sends to confirm it, yet his heart becomes hard and he does not let the people go.

sections.title: Boils Break Out on Man and Beast
sections.summary: Moses scatters ashes from a furnace toward heaven, and boils break out on man and beast throughout Egypt. The magicians cannot even stand before Moses, and “the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh” (Exodus 9:12), just as He had told Moses.

sections.title: The LORD Declares His Purpose and Warns of Hail
sections.summary: The LORD tells Pharaoh that He has raised him up to show His power, “and that My name may be declared in all the earth” (Exodus 9:16), and announces a very heavy hail for the next day. Those of Pharaoh’s servants who fear the word of the LORD bring their servants and livestock into shelter, while those who disregard it leave them in the field.

sections.title: Hail and Fire Fall on Egypt but Not on Goshen
sections.summary: Moses stretches out his rod, and the LORD sends thunder, hail, and fire, striking people, animals, plants, and trees throughout Egypt. “Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was no hail” (Exodus 9:26).

sections.title: Pharaoh Confesses Sin and Hardens His Heart Again
sections.summary: Pharaoh says, “I have sinned this time. The LORD is righteous, and my people and I are wicked” (Exodus 9:27), and Moses prays so that Pharaoh may know “that the earth is the LORD’s” (Exodus 9:29) while warning that Pharaoh and his servants still do not fear the LORD God. When the storm stops, Pharaoh sins yet more and hardens his heart, he and his servants.

1.brief: The LORD sends Moses to Pharaoh with the word of the God of the Hebrews: “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” The demand is repeated before the fifth plague.
1.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Go in to Pharaoh and tell him,”

The fifth plague begins, like the others, with God sending Moses back into the palace. Pharaoh has broken his word twice (8:15, 32), but God still speaks to him before He strikes.

“Thus says the LORD God of the Hebrews: ‘Let My people go, that they may serve Me.”

God again names Himself by His tie to the despised Hebrews, and the demand is unchanged. The issue remains the same: Israel belongs to the LORD and must be free to serve Him.

2.brief: The LORD addresses Pharaoh’s refusal to let them go and his continued hold on them. The warning that follows depends on whether Pharaoh keeps holding Israel.
2.explain:
“For if you refuse to let them go, and still hold them,”

The warning turns on Pharaoh’s choice. The word “hold” pictures a tight grip. Pharaoh is not merely failing to release Israel. He is clutching them. What follows depends on whether he keeps holding on.

3.brief: The hand of the LORD will be on Pharaoh’s cattle in the field, horses, donkeys, camels, oxen, and sheep, with “a very severe pestilence.” The plague will strike Egypt’s working animals and wealth.
3.explain:
“behold, the hand of the LORD will be on your cattle in the field,”

The plague will come from “the hand of the LORD” directly. This is the first time the phrase appears in the plagues. No rod is mentioned for this plague. God Himself will strike.

The target is livestock “in the field,” animals out at pasture. That detail matters for understanding 9:6.

“on the horses, on the donkeys, on the camels, on the oxen, and on the sheep—a very severe pestilence.”

The list covers Egypt’s working animals and its wealth: horses for chariots, donkeys and camels for transport, oxen for plowing, sheep for wool and food. A “very severe pestilence” would cripple farming, trade, and transport.
3.notes: Camels are sometimes said to be out of place in Egypt at this period. Evidence for their use in the ancient Near East is debated, but the text lists them among Egypt’s livestock, and they would not have been the main animal in view.

4.brief: The LORD will make a difference between Israel’s livestock and Egypt’s, so that nothing belonging to Israel will die. God’s protection of His people extends even to their animals.
4.explain:
“And the LORD will make a difference between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt.”

As with the flies (8:22–23), God will distinguish Israel from Egypt. This time the distinction reaches even to the animals.

“So nothing shall die of all that belongs to the children of Israel.”

The promise is complete: “nothing shall die” that belongs to Israel. God’s protection of His people extends even to their flocks and herds.

5.brief: The LORD sets a time, saying, “Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land.” Naming the time in advance makes clear that the plague comes from the LORD.
5.explain:
“Then the LORD appointed a set time, saying, ‘Tomorrow the LORD will do this thing in the land.”

God names the day in advance. If the animals died on the announced day, and only Egypt’s animals, no one could call it chance or ordinary disease. Naming the time makes clear that the plague comes from the LORD.

6.brief: The next day the LORD does it, “all the livestock of Egypt died,” but not one of Israel’s livestock dies. God’s word is fulfilled exactly, including the distinction between the peoples.
6.explain:
“So the LORD did this thing on the next day, and all the livestock of Egypt died;”

God did what He said, on the day He said. The word “all” should be read with 9:3. The plague struck the livestock in the field. Later the Egyptians still had animals to bring in from the hail (9:19–21), so “all” here means all within the scope God announced, or all kinds of livestock, not every single animal in Egypt.

“but of the livestock of the children of Israel, not one died.”

The contrast is total. Egypt’s herds died, and “not one” of Israel’s animals died. God’s word was fulfilled exactly, including the distinction between the peoples.
6.notes: The Hebrew word for “all” often means all of a kind or a large group, not every single individual. The context of 9:3 and 9:19–21 shows that limited sense here.

7.brief: Pharaoh sends to check and finds that not one of Israel’s animals has died, yet his heart becomes hard, and he does not let the people go. Pharaoh sees the evidence of God’s hand and still refuses.
7.explain:
“Then Pharaoh sent, and indeed, not even one of the livestock of the Israelites was dead.”

Pharaoh sent to check. He wanted to know whether the distinction was real. His messengers found that “not even one” of Israel’s animals had died. He had the evidence he needed.

“But the heart of Pharaoh became hard, and he did not let the people go.”

Even with the proof in hand, Pharaoh did not yield. His heart “became hard.” Pharaoh saw the evidence of God’s hand and still refused. Evidence alone does not change a heart set against God.
7.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “became hard” here means to become heavy, the same root used in 7:14 and 8:15, 32.

8.brief: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron to take handfuls of ashes from a furnace and have Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh. The sixth plague, like the third, comes without warning.
8.explain:
“So the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, ‘Take for yourselves handfuls of ashes from a furnace,”

The sixth plague, like the third, comes without warning. God tells the brothers to take “ashes from a furnace,” most likely a kiln where bricks were fired or a furnace used in Egypt’s industry.

“and let Moses scatter it toward the heavens in the sight of Pharaoh.”

Moses is to throw the ashes into the air “in the sight of Pharaoh.” The sign is done publicly so that Pharaoh sees where the plague comes from.
8.notes: Some interpreters see a fitting irony in the furnace ashes: the kilns that fired the bricks Israel was forced to make become the source of Egypt’s affliction. The text does not draw this connection, so it remains a suggestion.

9.brief: The ashes will become fine dust over Egypt and cause boils that break out in sores on man and beast. The judgment now touches the bodies of the Egyptians themselves.
9.explain:
“And it will become fine dust in all the land of Egypt,”

The handfuls of ash will spread as “fine dust” across the whole land. A small act brings a nationwide result.

“and it will cause boils that break out in sores on man and beast throughout all the land of Egypt.”

The dust will cause “boils that break out in sores.” The Hebrew describes inflamed, festering swellings that burst into open sores. The judgment now touches the bodies of the Egyptians themselves, and their animals as well.
9.notes: The Hebrew word translated “boils” is used of Job’s affliction (Job 2:7) and of Hezekiah’s sickness (2 Kings 20:7). Deuteronomy 28:27 warns of “the boils of Egypt” as a covenant curse.

10.brief: Moses and Aaron take the ashes and stand before Pharaoh, Moses scatters them toward heaven, and boils break out on man and beast. The plague begins in Pharaoh’s presence.
10.explain:
“Then they took ashes from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh,”

The brothers obeyed and stood “before Pharaoh.”

“and Moses scattered them toward heaven. And they caused boils that break out in sores on man and beast.”

The result followed at once. The plague began in Pharaoh’s presence, so he could not doubt its source.

11.brief: The magicians cannot stand before Moses because of the boils, “for the boils were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians.” The men who once imitated the signs are now afflicted themselves and cannot even stand before Moses.
11.explain:
“And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils,”

The magicians had imitated the first two plagues (7:22; 8:7) and failed at the third (8:18). Now they cannot even “stand before Moses.” They may have been too sick to appear at court, or too humiliated. Either way, Egypt’s experts have left the contest.

“for the boils were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians.”

The men who once imitated the signs are now afflicted themselves. Their arts could not protect even their own bodies.

12.brief: “But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh,” and he did not heed them, just as the LORD had told Moses. For the first time the narrator says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, as He announced in Exodus 4:21.
12.explain:
“But the LORD hardened the heart of Pharaoh;”

For the first time, the narrator says directly that “the LORD hardened” Pharaoh’s heart. God had announced this from the beginning (4:21; 7:3). Pharaoh has repeatedly hardened his own heart (8:15, 32). Now God confirms him in the course he has chosen. Pharaoh remains responsible for his refusal, and God carries out His judgment through it.

“and he did not heed them, just as the LORD had spoken to Moses.”

Nothing is out of God’s control. Pharaoh’s refusal unfolds “just as the LORD had spoken.”
12.notes: Before this verse, the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart is described either as Pharaoh’s own act (8:15, 32) or without naming who hardened it (7:13, 22; 8:19; 9:7). From here on, God is named as hardening Pharaoh in several places (10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8), though Pharaoh hardens his own heart once more (9:34).

13.brief: The LORD tells Moses to rise early and stand before Pharaoh with the word of the God of the Hebrews: “Let My people go, that they may serve Me.” The seventh plague begins with the longest warning yet.
13.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh,”

God sends Moses again at dawn, as before the first and fourth plagues (7:15; 8:20).

“and say to him, ‘Thus says the LORD God of the Hebrews: ‘Let My people go, that they may serve Me,”

The same demand comes again. The seventh plague begins with the longest warning yet, extending through 9:19.

14.brief: God says He will now send all His plagues on Pharaoh, his servants, and his people, “that you may know that there is none like Me in all the earth.” The coming judgments aim to show the LORD’s uniqueness.
14.explain:
“for at this time I will send all My plagues to your very heart, and on your servants and on your people,”

God announces that the judgments will now intensify. “All My plagues” will strike “your very heart,” Pharaoh himself, as well as his officials and people. The phrase may mean that the blows will now reach Pharaoh at his core.

“that you may know that there is none like Me in all the earth.”

The purpose is that Pharaoh will learn “there is none like Me.” Pharaoh asked, “Who is the LORD?” (5:2). The answer is that no god anywhere compares with Him. The coming judgments aim to show the LORD’s uniqueness.

15.brief: God says that if He had already struck Pharaoh and his people with pestilence, they would have been cut off from the earth. Pharaoh is still alive only because God has held back the full force of His judgment.
15.explain:
“Now if I had stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with pestilence,”

God speaks of what He could have done. He could have struck Pharaoh and his people with the same “pestilence” that killed the livestock.

“then you would have been cut off from the earth.”

If God had done so, Egypt would have been wiped out. Pharaoh is still alive only because God has held back the full force of His judgment.
15.notes: The Hebrew verbs in this verse can be read as describing what God could have done already (as in the NKJV) or what He could do now. The NKJV reading fits the explanation God gives in 9:16 for why He has not.

16.brief: God declares, “for this purpose I have raised you up, that I may show My power in you, and that My name may be declared in all the earth.” God has kept Pharaoh standing so that His power and name may be made known everywhere.
16.explain:
“But indeed for this purpose I have raised you up,”

God explains why Pharaoh is still standing. “For this purpose I have raised you up.” The phrase means God has kept Pharaoh in his position and allowed him to remain alive. Pharaoh’s survival is not a sign that he has escaped God. It serves God’s purpose.

“that I may show My power in you, and that My name may be declared in all the earth.”

The purpose is twofold. God will “show My power” through His dealings with Pharaoh, and His “name” will be “declared in all the earth.” The deliverance from Egypt would become known far beyond Egypt. Rahab in Jericho later told the spies, “we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea for you when you came out of Egypt” (Joshua 2:10). God has kept Pharaoh standing so that His power and name may be made known everywhere.
16.notes:
Paul quotes this verse in Romans 9:17: “For this very purpose I have raised you up.” The Greek translation of Exodus reads differently here, roughly “you were preserved.” In Exodus 9:15–16 the point is that God had kept Pharaoh alive instead of cutting him off. Paul’s own wording, “raised you up,” stands closer to the Hebrew.

The Hebrew verb translated “raised you up” means to cause to stand. It can mean to keep someone standing, that is, to preserve him alive.

17.brief: God says Pharaoh still exalts himself against His people by refusing to let them go. Pharaoh’s refusal is pride set against God and His people.
17.explain:
“As yet you exalt yourself against My people in that you will not let them go.”

God names Pharaoh’s attitude. Pharaoh sets himself up like a barrier or a raised road “against My people.” Pharaoh’s refusal is pride set against God and His people.
17.notes: The Hebrew verb translated “exalt yourself” is related to a word for a raised highway or siege ramp. It pictures Pharaoh building himself up as an obstacle.

18.brief: God announces that tomorrow at this time He will send very heavy hail, such as Egypt has never seen since its founding. The coming storm will be unmatched in Egypt’s history.
18.explain:
“Behold, tomorrow about this time I will cause very heavy hail to rain down,”

God sets the time precisely: “tomorrow about this time.” He will send “very heavy hail.” Hail and severe storms were rare in Egypt, which made the plague all the more striking.

“such as has not been in Egypt since its founding until now.”

The storm will be unmatched in Egypt’s history. No Egyptian record or memory will compare with it.

19.brief: God tells Pharaoh to send and bring in all livestock and everything in the field, for whatever is left outside will die. Even in judgment God gives a warning that allows people to take shelter.
19.explain:
“Therefore send now and gather your livestock and all that you have in the field,”

God gives a way of escape. Pharaoh is to bring in “your livestock and all that you have in the field.” Even in judgment God gives a warning that allows people to take shelter.

“for the hail shall come down on every man and every animal which is found in the field and is not brought home; and they shall die.”

The danger is deadly. Whatever stays outside will die. God’s mercy and God’s judgment stand side by side in this warning.
19.notes: The command to gather the livestock shows that Egypt still had animals after the pestilence of 9:6, confirming that “all the livestock” there referred to the animals in the field.

20.brief: Those among Pharaoh’s servants who “feared the word of the LORD” make their servants and livestock flee into the houses. Some Egyptians take God’s warning seriously and act on it.
20.explain:
“He who feared the word of the LORD among the servants of Pharaoh”

For the first time, some Egyptians respond to God’s word. Some of Pharaoh’s own officials “feared the word of the LORD.” They took it seriously enough to act.

“made his servants and his livestock flee to the houses.”

They brought their workers and animals indoors. Some Egyptians took God’s warning seriously and acted on it. Their response shows what taking the LORD’s word seriously looks like.

21.brief: But those who do not regard the word of the LORD leave their servants and livestock in the field. The different responses show how people treat God’s word.
21.explain:
“But he who did not regard the word of the LORD left his servants and his livestock in the field.”

Others “did not regard the word of the LORD.” They did not take it to heart. They left their workers and animals outside. The different responses show how people treat God’s word. The same warning reached everyone, and each household chose how to answer it.
21.notes: The phrase “did not regard” reads literally did not set his heart to. The same expression describes Pharaoh in 7:23, “Neither was his heart moved by this.”

22.brief: The LORD tells Moses to stretch out his hand toward heaven so that hail will fall on man, beast, and every plant throughout Egypt. The judgment is about to fall as announced.
22.explain:
“Then the LORD said to Moses, ‘Stretch out your hand toward heaven,”

Moses is to lift his hand “toward heaven,” the source of the storm.

“that there may be hail in all the land of Egypt—on man, on beast, and on every herb of the field, throughout the land of Egypt.”

The hail will strike people, animals, and plants. The judgment is about to fall as announced.

23.brief: Moses stretches out his rod toward heaven, and the LORD sends thunder and hail, with fire darting to the ground. The LORD Himself sends the storm at Moses’ signal.
23.explain:
“And Moses stretched out his rod toward heaven;”

Moses obeyed, raising the rod.

“and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire darted to the ground. And the LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt.”

The verse twice names “the LORD” as the One who sent the storm. Moses gave the signal, but God sent “thunder and hail,” and “fire,” most likely lightning, “darted to the ground.” The LORD Himself sends the storm at Moses’ signal.
23.notes: The Hebrew word translated “thunder” is literally “voices.” The storm is described as the voice of God, a picture found also in Psalm 29:3–9.

24.brief: Hail with fire mingled in it falls so heavily that there has been nothing like it in Egypt since it became a nation. The storm matches God’s warning in verse 18.
24.explain:
“So there was hail, and fire mingled with the hail,”

The storm combined hail with lightning, “fire mingled with the hail.”

“so very heavy that there was none like it in all the land of Egypt since it became a nation.”

The storm matched God’s warning in 9:18. Nothing like it had ever been seen in Egypt.

25.brief: The hail strikes everything in the field throughout Egypt, both man and beast, every plant, and every tree. The destruction falls on all who ignored the warning.
25.explain:
“And the hail struck throughout the whole land of Egypt, all that was in the field, both man and beast;”

Everything left outside was struck. People and animals in the open died, as God had warned (9:19).

“and the hail struck every herb of the field and broke every tree of the field.”

Crops were flattened and trees “broke.” The destruction fell on all who ignored the warning and on the land itself.

26.brief: “Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was no hail.” God’s distinction between His people and Egypt continues in the midst of the storm.
26.explain:
“Only in the land of Goshen, where the children of Israel were, there was no hail.”

One region was untouched. In “the land of Goshen,” where Israel lived, the sky was clear. God’s distinction between His people and Egypt continued in the midst of the storm.

27.brief: Pharaoh calls Moses and Aaron and says, “I have sinned this time. The LORD is righteous, and my people and I are wicked.” Under the pressure of judgment Pharaoh admits guilt and acknowledges the LORD’s righteousness.
27.explain:
“And Pharaoh sent and called for Moses and Aaron, and said to them, ‘I have sinned this time.”

For the first time Pharaoh confesses sin. “I have sinned this time.” The words sound humble, but “this time” may suggest he sees this as a single lapse rather than a pattern of rebellion.

“The LORD is righteous, and my people and I are wicked.”

Pharaoh even declares “The LORD is righteous.” Under the pressure of judgment, Pharaoh admits guilt and acknowledges the LORD’s righteousness. The question is whether his words reflect a changed heart. What follows will show.

28.brief: Pharaoh asks them to entreat the LORD to stop the thunder and hail and promises, “I will let you go.” He again promises freedom in exchange for relief.
28.explain:
“Entreat the LORD, that there may be no more mighty thundering and hail, for it is enough.”

Pharaoh asks Moses to pray. “It is enough.” He wants the storm to stop. The phrase “mighty thundering” reads literally voices of God.

“I will let you go, and you shall stay no longer.”

Pharaoh promises again: “I will let you go.” He again promises freedom in exchange for relief.

29.brief: Moses agrees to spread out his hands to the LORD once he leaves the city so that the storm will stop, “that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s.” The ending of the plague will itself reveal the LORD’s ownership of the earth.
29.explain:
“So Moses said to him, ‘As soon as I have gone out of the city, I will spread out my hands to the LORD;”

Moses agrees to pray. To “spread out my hands” was a posture of prayer, palms lifted toward God.

“the thunder will cease, and there will be no more hail, that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s.”

The ending of the storm will teach Pharaoh that “the earth is the LORD’s.” The land of Egypt does not belong to Pharaoh or to Egypt’s gods. The ending of the plague will itself reveal the LORD’s ownership of the earth (compare Psalm 24:1).

30.brief: Moses tells Pharaoh plainly, “I know that you will not yet fear the LORD God.” Moses sees that Pharaoh’s confession is not true repentance.
30.explain:
“But as for you and your servants, I know that you will not yet fear the LORD God.”

Moses sees through the confession. “I know that you will not yet fear the LORD God.” Pharaoh has admitted sin under pressure, but he does not revere God. Acknowledging sin is not the same as yielding to God. Moses sees that Pharaoh’s confession is not true repentance.

31.brief: The flax and barley are struck, because the barley was in the head and the flax in bud. The note shows the extent of the damage to Egypt’s crops.
31.explain:
“Now the flax and the barley were struck, for the barley was in the head and the flax was in bud.”

The narrator adds a note on the damage. “The flax and the barley were struck.” The barley had formed its heads of grain, and the flax was in bloom. Both crops were ruined. Flax supplied linen, and barley was a staple grain.
31.notes: In Egypt, barley and flax ripened earlier than wheat, usually in late winter or early spring. The note helps place the plague within the agricultural year.

32.brief: The wheat and spelt are not struck because they are late crops. Some of Egypt’s harvest remains, which the locusts will later consume.
32.explain:
“But the wheat and the spelt were not struck, for they are late crops.”

“The wheat and the spelt” survived because they ripened later. Some of Egypt’s harvest remained, which the locusts would later consume (10:5, 15).
32.notes: The Hebrew word translated “spelt” refers to a kind of wheat. Its exact identification is uncertain.

33.brief: Moses goes out of the city, spreads out his hands to the LORD, and the thunder, hail, and rain stop. God answers Moses’ prayer, just as He did with the earlier plagues.
33.explain:
“So Moses went out of the city from Pharaoh and spread out his hands to the LORD;”

Moses did exactly what he said. He left the city and prayed.

“then the thunder and the hail ceased, and the rain was not poured on the earth.”

The storm stopped. God answered Moses’ prayer, just as He did with the earlier plagues.

34.brief: When Pharaoh sees that the storm has stopped, “he sinned yet more; and he hardened his heart, he and his servants.” Pharaoh’s relapse shows that his confession was only words, and his servants share his hardness.
34.explain:
“And when Pharaoh saw that the rain, the hail, and the thunder had ceased,”

As soon as the danger passed, Pharaoh’s attitude changed.

“he sinned yet more; and he hardened his heart, he and his servants.”

Pharaoh “sinned yet more.” The man who had just said, “I have sinned,” sinned again. He “hardened his heart,” and his “servants” joined him. Pharaoh’s relapse showed that his confession was only words, and his servants shared his hardness. The narrator tests the confession by the response that follows.

35.brief: Pharaoh’s heart is hard, and he does not let Israel go, “as the LORD had spoken by Moses.” The chapter ends as God foretold, with Pharaoh still refusing.
35.explain:
“So the heart of Pharaoh was hard;”

The chapter closes with a summary. Pharaoh’s heart “was hard.”

“neither would he let the children of Israel go, as the LORD had spoken by Moses.”

Pharaoh still refused, “as the LORD had spoken by Moses.” The chapter ends as God foretold.
35.notes: The Hebrew verb in this verse is the one meaning to be strong or firm (as in 7:13). The verb in 9:34 means to make heavy. Exodus uses several verbs for the hardening without sharply distinguishing them.
